extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and readers of political theory and public opinion; policymakers interested in democratic institutions
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading and extraction of normative/practical principles about how public opinion, representative institutions, patronage, and proposed alternatives (e.g., guild socialism) succeed or fail. Emphasis on informational, institutional, and coercive conditions for functioning democracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-contained community assumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic theory in a 'self-contained community' assumes that 'the environment was so familiar that one could take it for granted that men were talking about substantially the same things' — facts and moral codes are obvious and equally accessible, so differences are only in judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text explains that in such communities there is 'no need to guarantee the sources of information' and 'the community could take its supply of information for granted'; reasoning errors would be quickly exposed in free discussion. This functions as an implicit criterion for when democratic deliberation will reliably produce truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for instruments of knowledge for democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracy requires instruments of knowledge for reporting its environment; lacking these, democratic theory had to 'fall back upon the wisdom and experience' accumulated locally in voters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author emphasizes that without systematic reporting and shared information, national decision-making cannot rely on local impressions alone. This criterion distinguishes contexts where self-governing assumptions hold from those needing institutional information-gathering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checks-and-balances as a remedy for fragmented public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine of checks and balances was intended to 'neutralize local opinion' and substitute 'the mild influence of the magistracy' for 'the sanguinary agency of the sword' — enabling government to be enabled to control the governed and obliged to control itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Madison: 'Ambition must be made to counteract ambition.' The guidance explains that the constitutional design aimed to deadlock local/class interests so they wouldn't obstruct national government; this is presented as an explicit institutional criterion for managing dispersed public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of patronage and fiscal measures to bind elites to the Union
rubrics_metrics.description: Patronage and fiscal measures (e.g., Hamilton's fiscal policies) were used to attach provincial notables, gentry, creditors, manufacturers and traders to the new national government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues Hamilton 'used class privileges to make the Union' — patronage and economic policy served as instruments to secure cooperation where common information and sentiment did not suffice. This is a pragmatic criterion for building national cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rotation in office and its unintended effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Rotation in office (short terms, removal on party grounds) was seen as democratic reform but produced a new governing class and professional politicians instead of the small-town ideal of temporary civic service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although rotation 'acknowledged the new dignity of the average man,' in a national context it created entrenched party machinery and the professional politician. This illustrates an anti-pattern: transplanting township practices to a national scale without institutional adaptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: When shared information is absent, cooperation depends on force, patronage, or privilege
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a 'common consciousness' (shared knowledge of national circumstances and reasons of state) does not exist, association among large groups will depend either on force or on milder mechanisms like patronage and privilege.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author frames this as a diagnostic criterion for state-building: the degree to which material for a common consciousness exists determines whether cooperation will rest on coercion or on patronage/privilege. Implication: institutional design must address informational foundations, or else rely on coercive/patrimonial mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional informational deficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: A congress of representatives is 'essentially a group of blind men in a vast, unknown world' because there is 'no systematic, and authorized way for Congress to know what is going on in the world'; exchanging local opinions is insufficient for translocal or foreign policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion diagnoses the limits of representative assemblies: without instruments for controlled reporting and objective analysis, legislation becomes either the work of insiders or a bundle of local items (pork). The text recommends institutional remedies (see related items).

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for controlled reporting and objective analysis in lawmaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Lawmakers need instruments for controlled reporting and objective analysis—analogous to an accountant's cost sheets—to understand subtle and hidden effects of laws; putting together a mosaic of local pictures is inadequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage provides an analogy: a factory head cannot rely on the foreman alone but needs data. This functions as an explicit prescription for what institutional information capacity is required for sound national policymaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential informational advantage is one-sided and censoring
rubrics_metrics.description: The President, 'presiding over a vast collection of bureaus and their agents,' can inform Congress but 'he tells Congress what he chooses to tell it'; the relationship is 'wholly one-sided and tricky' and subject to executive censorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion highlights a structural asymmetry: executive informational control can leave legislators starved for facts, forcing them to rely on private tips, press disclosures, or formal investigations. It implies a need to diversify and institutionalize information flows to the legislature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional investigations as substitute and their pathologies
rubrics_metrics.description: Because Congress lacks regular informational instruments, it resorts to 'the legalized atrocity, the Congressional investigation,' which becomes a 'wild and feverish man-hunt' and yields little systematic information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text treats investigations as brittle, episodic diagnostics rather than steady informational mechanisms. This is presented as an anti-pattern for informed policymaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logrolling and localism in legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: Absent effective means of information and analysis, a legislature 'must oscillate between blind regularity, occasional insurgency, and logrolling' — resulting in laws broken into local items (tariff schedules, post offices, pensions) enacted for local reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies logrolling as the political mechanism that makes legislative regularity palatable and as symptomatic of failure to form national consensus based on common information. It functions as a criterion for assessing the national character of legislation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patronage and local subsidies stabilize special local opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: Patronage, subsidies, and privileges attach political chieftains to national government and 'stabilize thousands of special opinions, local discontents, private ambitions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage treats patronage as both stabilizing (weaning leaders to national interests) and corrupting (creating local clientelism). This dual effect is an evaluative criterion for the role of patronage in state cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two alternatives when self-centered groups conflict: coercion or elaborate information/institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: When self-centered groups cannot cooperate, the alternatives are (1) government by terror/coercion, or (2) a highly developed system of information, analysis, and self-consciousness that makes 'knowledge of national circumstances and reasons of state' evident to all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This frames a planning criterion for large-scale association: either build coercive structures or invest in institutions that produce shared knowledge. Practical state-building requires assessing which path is feasible given informational infrastructure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guild socialism must account for coercive powers it appears to reject
rubrics_metrics.description: Although Guild Socialism aspires to be 'not an instrument of coercion,' the Commune as described by Cole exercises many powers (fixes prices, allocates resources and labor-power, levies taxes, controls armed forces, appoints judges, runs police) which are inherently coercive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author uses Cole's own enumeration of powers to argue that guild socialism, if implemented, would still possess coercive instruments; this functions as a normative test of whether a political model truly reduces coercion or merely reshapes it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abolition of capitalist property alone is insufficient—institutions required to maintain equality
rubrics_metrics.description: The guildsmen do not expect a miracle from the disappearance of capitalist property; they insist on 'getting the mechanism right' and providing institutions for maintaining the equilibrium and expressing 'men's social wills.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a substantive criterion for evaluating utopian institutional proposals: they must propose durable mechanisms for sustaining equality and representation, not merely assume equality will remove motives to aggression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factory/shop as the appropriate unit for industrial democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Guild socialists argue the 'factory' (more precisely, the shop or workshop where workers are in personal contact) is the natural democratic unit for industrial self-government and should be the basis of guild representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text cautions about scale: 'a large plant, a railway system, a great coal field, is not a natural unit' — so proposals must justify unit size and mechanisms for coordinating larger structures without losing direct self-government. This is a criterion for institutional design in industrial democracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition problem: acknowledgement that establishing new order may require direct action or coercion
rubrics_metrics.description: Cole acknowledges that the new guild society 'cannot be brought into existence by universal consent' and that a period of direct action by trade unions (and potential civil conflict) may be required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This functions as a realist test of transformation proposals: any plan to restructure society must address how the transition will occur and what coercive or disruptive steps might be necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of transplanting small-community democratic images to national/industrial scale
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic images derived from the self-contained village or township fail when applied directly to national or industrial scales; concepts like rotation in office and local self-government produce unintended results when scaled up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The recurring evaluative point is that institutional prescriptions must be sensitive to scale and informational differences; failure to do so produces pathologies such as entrenched party machines or ineffective national legislatures.
